lead.s: Paediatrics end of 2nd semester exam (MBPE 4300): 5 October 2021, 50 MCQs

b: Caused by Vibrio cholerae (Gram-negative bacterium)
Transmission: faecal-oral route, contaminated water/food
Colonises small intestine, does not invade mucosa
Produces cholera toxin (CT) : irreversibly activates adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP in enterocytes → massive Cl⁻ secretion (via CFTR) → passive Na⁺ and water movement into lumen
Abrupt onset of watery diarrhoea (rice-water stools)

qs.q: The molecular basis for effect of cholera toxin on duodenal mucosa cells is
o: Ribosylation of guanosine triphosphate binding protein
Increased ability of potassium membrane transport pumps
Activation of cellular adenylate cyclase enzyme activity
Inactivation of cellular G1 regulatory protein function
Increased generation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate
qs.e: Cholera toxin's A subunit ADP-ribosylates the Gsα protein (GTP-binding protein), locking it in the active state. This permanently activates adenylate cyclase, causing continuous cAMP production, which drives massive chloride and water secretion into the intestinal lumen.

qs.q: The molecular basis for cholera toxin's effect on duodenal cells is
qs.e: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, preventing GTPase activity and leading to continuous adenylyl cyclase activation and cAMP production.

qs.q: The first microorganism to satisfy Koch's postulates (in the late 19th century) was Vibrio cholerae, responsible for cholera.
qs.e: Robert Koch successfully applied his postulates to demonstrate that Vibrio cholerae was the causative agent of cholera. This was a landmark achievement in microbiology and epidemiology.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Cholera is an acute secretory diarrhoea caused by Vibrio cholerae toxin that drives massive intestinal fluid loss. Prompt rehydration and targeted antibiotics prevent death.

sections.p: Cholera is a watery diarrhoea syndrome caused by ingestion of Vibrio cholerae producing cholera toxin. Diagnosis rests on clinical picture plus stool culture or rapid antigen test.
b: Rapid onset of profuse rice‑water stools
History of contaminated water/food exposure
Positive stool culture for V. cholerae O1/O139

t.b: Does the patient have V. cholerae? Positive result confirms cholera; negative does not exclude early infection.
Is the diarrhoea secretory? Gap <50 mOsm/kg supports secretory (cholera) diarrhoea.

sections.p: Severity is graded by dehydration status and volume loss, using WHO criteria: no, some, or severe dehydration.
b: Severe dehydration: >10 % body weight loss, sunken eyes, rapid pulse
Some dehydration: 5‑10 % weight loss, thirst, reduced urine

sections.p: The primary cause is ingestion of V. cholerae‑contaminated water or food. Co‑factors that increase risk include poor sanitation, crowded settings, and co‑infection with HIV or malnutrition.
b: Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 (most common)
Contaminated surface water
Food washed with unsafe water

sections.p: Patients develop sudden profuse watery diarrhoea with a “rice‑water” appearance, abdominal cramps, and rapid dehydration. Fever is usually absent.
b: Watery, pale, non‑bloody stools
Vomiting may precede diarrhoea
Signs of dehydration develop within hours

sections.p: Investigations focus on confirming the pathogen, assessing dehydration, and detecting electrolyte disturbances.
b: Stool culture or rapid test for V. cholerae
Serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine

t.b: Are there hyponatraemia or hypokalaemia? Low Na⁺/K⁺ guide rehydration fluid composition.
Is renal perfusion compromised? Elevated BUN indicates severe dehydration.

sections.p: Rapid fluid loss can lead to hypovolemic shock, acute kidney injury, and metabolic acidosis. Early recognition prevents mortality.
b: Shock (cold, clammy skin, hypotension)
Altered mental status
Oliguria or anuria

sections.p: Rehydration is the cornerstone; replace losses with oral rehydration solution (ORS) or IV fluids for severe cases. A single dose of doxycycline or azithromycin shortens illness.
b: ORS for mild‑moderate dehydration (WHO formula)
IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration
Single‑dose doxycycline (or azithromycin) to eradicate bacteria

sections.p: Observe for re‑hydration success, repeat electrolytes, and educate on safe water. Vaccination and water sanitation reduce outbreaks.
b: Check urine output and mental status after rehydration
Advise boiled or treated water, hand hygiene
Oral cholera vaccine for high‑risk areas

sections.p: Other causes of acute watery diarrhoea can mimic cholera but differ in pathogen and management.
b: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) – similar exposure, no specific antibiotic need
Giardiasis – foul‑smelling stools, chronic course
Vibrio parahaemolyticus – seafood‑related, usually milder

sections.p: Stool microscopy may miss V. cholerae if sampling is delayed; normal leukocyte count does not rule out cholera because it is non‑inflammatory.
b: Negative stool culture after >48 h of antibiotics may be false‑negative
Normal white blood cell count despite severe dehydration

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, rapid pulse, low blood pressure)

faq.q: Why does cholera cause watery diarrhoea even when fasting?
faq.a: Cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase, forcing chloride secretion via CFTR; water follows osmotically regardless of food intake.
Antibiotics shorten illness and reduce transmission but are not needed if rehydration is prompt and the disease is mild.

faq.q: Can cholera be prevented without a vaccine?
faq.a: Yes, by ensuring safe drinking water, proper sanitation, and hand hygiene.

exam: Describe the pathophysiology of cholera toxin and its effect on intestinal secretion.
Outline the WHO dehydration classification and corresponding rehydration strategy for cholera.
List the first‑line antimicrobial agents for cholera and explain why they are preferred.
